title: Take a proportionate stand on one small unfairness

sections.title: Understand the distinction
sections.body: Moral courage concerns a justified action under a real cost or fear. Analyzing what courage means is preparation; making a stand requires an actual appropriate act and its consequences, which fiction cannot supply for the reader.

sections.title: Complete fictional practice material
sections.body: Complete private document extract: “Lee wrote and designed the notice.” Contribution log: Lee wrote; Mo designed. Mo consents to accurate credit, not public confrontation. Editor Uma invites corrections by 16:00. Jo fears mild disagreement but has authority only to request a correction, not edit the published file.

sections.title: Work through the supplied case
sections.body: Write the evidence-based request and a proportionate follow-up if declined. Record the actual social cost only in a real route; use the supplied response as case analysis.

sections.title: Try a different case before checking
sections.body: A person privately rehearses a justified objection but never has a safe opportunity to raise it. What can they report?

checks.title: Compare reasoning and review the supplied result
checks.body: Ask Uma to compare the log and change the credit to text by Lee/layout by Mo. Later fiction: Uma first says it is not worth changing; Jo restates the documented contribution once, and Uma corrects it at 15:50. That depicts a bounded stand, not a real action by the learner. Partial: silently revise one’s private copy. Incorrect: publicly accuse Lee of intentional theft. Higher risk requires another suitable route, not compulsory confrontation.
criteria: The stand rests on verified case facts
Method fits authority and affected preferences
Preparation is not credited as performed courage

checks.title: Check the changed case
checks.body: Prepared wording and reasoning, with the actual stand unperformed. Lack of safe opportunity is not proof of cowardice; seek a suitable supported route or defer.
